The Maestro · Part 14 · Phase 3 · 🛡️ Safety lead · 💼 founder hat

Approvals and Compliance

Maestro-1 works (Part 12) and is defended (Part 13). Before anyone outside the company uses it, Gopala has to answer to three audiences: regulators, customers' security and legal teams, and his own release gate. This part maps what the EU AI Act asks of a general-purpose model provider and where Maestro-1 sits (with a script that does the arithmetic), the voluntary frameworks customers ask about, the documents every release needs, customers' security reviews, and the release decision itself, which in the story first comes back no.

1. Mission log: weeks 50–60

Weeks 50–54 · Mapping
  • Maps obligations with counsel; writes ai_act_check.py; starts the documents.
Weeks 55–58 · Documents and reviews
  • Model card, data summary, copyright policy, security questionnaires from three partners.
Weeks 59–60 · Release reviews
  • First release review: no-go (section 10). Second, a week later: go, for design partners first.

2. Why approvals are a product feature

  • Enterprise customers buy evidence, not only capability.
    • Their security teams ask where data goes, who can access it, how the model was tested and what happens in an incident.
    • A start-up that answers in days instead of months closes deals faster.
  • Regulation sets a floor.
    • The EU AI Act applies to providers placing general-purpose models on the EU market, wherever they are based.
    • Other jurisdictions have their own rules; Gopala starts with the EU because its obligations for model providers are the most specific today and his partners operate there.

Three audiences, three kinds of evidence

🏛️ RegulatorsTechnical documentation, copyright policy, training-content summary
🏢 CustomersSecurity questionnaires, contracts, model card, audit reports
🚦 The release gateEvaluation, safety, gate log, rollback, sign-offs

Much of the same evidence serves all three.

3. The EU AI Act and general-purpose models

  • The key dates.
    • Obligations for general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers have applied since 2 August 2025.
    • Models already on the market before that date have until 2 August 2027.
    • The Commission's enforcement powers for GPAI start on 2 August 2026.
  • Duties for every GPAI provider.
    • Technical documentation of the model for the AI Office and national authorities.
    • Information for downstream providers who build on it.
    • A policy to comply with EU copyright law, including machine-readable opt-outs.
    • A public summary of the content used for training, using the Commission's template.
  • Extra duties above a compute threshold.
    • A model is presumed to have "systemic risk" if its cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs; the presumption can be rebutted and the Commission can designate models below it.
    • Those providers must also evaluate and adversarially test the model, assess and mitigate systemic risks, report serious incidents and ensure cybersecurity, and notify the Commission.
  • The voluntary Code of Practice.
    • Finalised on 10 July 2025, with chapters on transparency, copyright, and safety and security; signing it is one way to show compliance.

4. Where Maestro-1 sits

ai_act_check.py · Python 3, no dependencies
"""ai_act_check.py — where does Maestro-1 sit under the EU AI Act's
general-purpose AI (GPAI) rules? A planning aid, NOT legal advice.

Facts used: GPAI obligations apply from 2 August 2025; a model is
presumed to have systemic risk above 1e25 FLOPs of cumulative training
compute (rebuttable; the Commission can also designate models). Training
compute uses 6 x active params x tokens (Part 3); post-training adds a
little. Scale-up scenarios are hypothetical.
"""
THRESHOLD = 1e25
RUNS = {  # name: (active params, tokens)
    "Maestro-1 pre-training": (11.7e9, 10e12),
    "post-training + loop cycles (our estimate)": (11.7e9, 0.3e12),
}
BASE = ["technical documentation for the AI Office and downstream providers",
        "information and documentation for downstream providers integrating the model",
        "a policy to comply with EU copyright law, including opt-outs",
        "a public summary of the content used for training (Commission template)"]
SYSTEMIC = ["model evaluations including adversarial testing", "assess and mitigate systemic risks",
            "track and report serious incidents", "adequate cybersecurity protection"]

def main():
    total = 0
    for name, (n, d) in RUNS.items():
        f = 6 * n * d; total += f
        print(f"{name:44s} {f:.2e} FLOPs")
    print(f"{'cumulative':44s} {total:.2e} FLOPs = {total/THRESHOLD:.1%} of the 1e25 presumption threshold")
    print("obligations as a GPAI provider placing the model on the EU market:")
    for o in BASE: print("  -", o)
    for mult in (5, 10, 15):
        f = total * mult
        print(f"if a future run used {mult:2d}x the compute: {f:.1e} FLOPs -> "
              f"{'presumed systemic risk: add ' + str(len(SYSTEMIC)) + ' more duties and notify the Commission' if f > THRESHOLD else 'still below the threshold'}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 ai_act_check.py # planning aid, not legal advice Maestro-1 pre-training 7.02e+23 FLOPs post-training + loop cycles (our estimate) 2.11e+22 FLOPs cumulative 7.23e+23 FLOPs = 7.2% of the 1e25 presumption threshold obligations as a GPAI provider placing the model on the EU market: - technical documentation for the AI Office and downstream providers - information and documentation for downstream providers integrating the model - a policy to comply with EU copyright law, including opt-outs - a public summary of the content used for training (Commission template) if a future run used 5x the compute: 3.6e+24 FLOPs -> still below the threshold if a future run used 10x the compute: 7.2e+24 FLOPs -> still below the threshold if a future run used 15x the compute: 1.1e+25 FLOPs -> presumed systemic risk: add 4 more duties and notify the Commission

Maestro-1's training compute vs the systemic-risk presumption

Maestro-1 (pre-training + post-training)7.2e23 FLOPs (7%)
10× Maestro-17.2e24 (72%)
15× Maestro-11.1e25 (above)
Threshold1e25 FLOPs

Real output of ai_act_check.py (6·N·D estimate, 11.7B active parameters).

  • What it means.
    • Maestro-1 used about 7% of the compute that triggers the systemic-risk presumption, so it carries the four baseline duties, not the extra four.
    • A future model with about 15 times the compute would cross the line; that is a planning fact for Maestro-2, not a distant one.
    • The 7.02e23 here differs slightly from Part 3's 7.2e23 because Part 9 fixed the active size at 11.7B rather than 12B.
  • The baseline duties still take real work.
    • The training-content summary depends on Part 8's manifest; without it, this would take months.

  • Map once, answer many times.
    • Each control (for example "access to training data is logged") is written once with its evidence, then referenced from every framework and questionnaire that asks.

6. The documents every release needs

  • Model card.
    • Mitchell et al. (2019) proposed model cards: intended use, limitations, evaluation results across conditions.
    • His version adds confidence intervals from Part 12 and known safety weaknesses from Part 13.
model_card.md · model card outline · not executed for this article
# Maestro-1 — model card (outline)
## Model
- Developer: Maestro (start-up) · Version: 1.0 · Date: month 13
- Architecture: mixture-of-experts, 65.2B total / 11.7B active parameters
- Training compute: ~7.2e23 FLOPs (6·N·D estimate) · Context: 64K tokens
## Intended use
- Software-engineering assistance inside customers' own repositories, through agents with a tool guard
- Not intended for: unsupervised production changes, medical/legal advice, decisions about people
## Training data
- ~10T tokens: filtered web, permissively licensed code, maths, books, multilingual, verified skills
- Public summary: see data-summary.pdf (EU template) · opt-outs honoured
## Evaluation (harness v3, contamination-checked, 95% CIs)
- Partner held-out tasks: pass@1 ... [CI] vs Maestro-0 ... [CI]
- Public benchmarks: ... (with contamination notes)
## Safety
- Red-team attack success by category with Wilson intervals; known weaknesses listed
## Limitations
- Below frontier models on general knowledge; English-first; can still write insecure code
## Contact
- security@ and incidents@ addresses, response times
  • The other documents.
    • Training-content summary (EU template) and the internal data manifest (Part 8).
    • Copyright and opt-out policy.
    • Evaluation and safety reports.
    • The loop's gate log since the last release (Part 11).
    • Incident process and contacts.

7. Customer security reviews

  • Every partner sends a questionnaire; the questions repeat.
    • Where is our code processed and stored? (Named regions, the sandbox design.)
    • Is our data used to train your models? (Only verified skills, abstracted, under contract; never raw code.)
    • Who can access it? (Named roles, logged, break-glass only.)
    • How do you handle incidents? (Part 13's process with notification times.)
  • The contract matters as much as the controls.
    • Data processing terms, a clear statement of what is and is not trained on, and the right to have skills derived from their tasks removed.

8. The release review

  • A meeting with a checklist and a decision.
    • Attendees: Gopala (founder and safety lead), the evaluator hat's report, outside counsel, one partner representative.
    • The release check runs first; if it says no-go, the meeting is about the gaps.
release_check.py · Python 3, no dependencies; scenario manifest
"""release_check.py — the release gate for a model version.

Every item must exist and be signed before Maestro-1 ships to anyone.
The manifest below is the SCENARIO state at the first review: two items
are missing, so the answer is no.
"""
REQUIRED = {
    "model_card": "model card: intended use, limits, evaluation results with CIs",
    "eval_report": "evaluation report from the harness (Part 12), contamination checked",
    "safety_report": "safety evaluation and red-team summary (Part 13)",
    "data_summary": "public training-content summary (EU template) and data manifest",
    "copyright_policy": "copyright and opt-out policy",
    "gate_log": "loop gate decisions since the last release (Part 11)",
    "incident_process": "incident contact, severity levels, response times",
    "partner_signoff": "design partners reviewed on their own data",
    "rollback_plan": "previous version kept serving; rollback tested",
}
MANIFEST = {
    "model_card": {"done": True, "signed": "Gopala"},
    "eval_report": {"done": True, "signed": "Gopala"},
    "safety_report": {"done": True, "signed": "external red team + Gopala"},
    "data_summary": {"done": False, "signed": ""},
    "copyright_policy": {"done": True, "signed": "counsel"},
    "gate_log": {"done": True, "signed": "Gopala"},
    "incident_process": {"done": True, "signed": "Gopala"},
    "partner_signoff": {"done": True, "signed": ""},
    "rollback_plan": {"done": True, "signed": "Gopala"},
}

def main():
    missing = []
    for k, desc in REQUIRED.items():
        m = MANIFEST.get(k, {})
        ok = m.get("done") and m.get("signed")
        print(f"{'OK  ' if ok else 'MISS'} {desc}" + ("" if ok else f"  ({'not done' if not m.get('done') else 'not signed'})"))
        if not ok: missing.append(k)
    print("RELEASE: " + ("GO" if not missing else f"NO-GO, {len(missing)} item(s) open: {', '.join(missing)}"))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 release_check.py # scenario state at the first review OK model card: intended use, limits, evaluation results with CIs OK evaluation report from the harness (Part 12), contamination checked OK safety evaluation and red-team summary (Part 13) MISS public training-content summary (EU template) and data manifest (not done) OK copyright and opt-out policy OK loop gate decisions since the last release (Part 11) OK incident contact, severity levels, response times MISS design partners reviewed on their own data (not signed) OK previous version kept serving; rollback tested RELEASE: NO-GO, 2 item(s) open: data_summary, partner_signoff
  • The first review says no.
    • The public training-content summary was not finished, because two data sources in the manifest still lacked licence details.
    • One design partner had not yet reviewed the model on their own data.
  • What happened next.
    • The two sources were removed from the summary's scope after confirming they had been excluded from training; the summary was finished.
    • The partner ran their review in three days. The second review a week later said go, for design partners first.

10. A staged release

Who gets Maestro-1, and when

🤝Design partnersMonth 13.5; their own repositories, close support
🧪Pilot customersMonth 14.5; limited seats, weekly reviews
🌍General availabilityMonth 16+; only after pilot evidence

Each stage has its own gate; any severity-1 incident pauses the next stage.

  • Why staged.
    • Real usage finds problems no harness does; finding them with five partners is cheaper than with five hundred customers.
    • Phase 4 (Parts 15–18) covers serving, products and operations through these stages.

11. Personal data in customers' code

  • If client repositories contain personal data, data-protection law applies to processing it.
    • In the EU, the GDPR requires a written data processing agreement when a service provider processes personal data on a customer's behalf (Article 28).
    • The customer is usually the controller; Maestro acts as a processor for task execution.
  • What that means in practice.
    • A data processing agreement in every contract, listing sub-processors such as the GPU provider (Part 4).
    • Processing kept in agreed regions; deletion after the retention period; help with data-subject requests.
  • Training on derived skills needs its own legal basis and contract terms.
    • That is why skills are abstracted, scanned and contractually agreed (Parts 8 and 13), and why partners can ask for removal.

12. One evidence library

  • Every claim in every document points to a record.
    • "Benchmarks were removed from training data" links to Part 8's decontamination log.
    • "Updates are human-approved" links to Part 11's gate log.
    • "Access is logged" links to access-log samples.
  • Why it pays.
    • A questionnaire answered in hours, an auditor's request answered in a day, a regulator's question answered with records instead of reconstruction.

From records to documents

🗂️RecordsManifests, gate log, eval runs, access logs
🧾ControlsEach control written once with its evidence
📄DocumentsModel card, data summary, policies
📨AnswersRegulators, customers, auditors

Write the record when the work happens; documents become assembly, not archaeology.

13. The compliance calendar

WhenWhat
Every releaseRelease check, model card update, data summary update if training data changed
Every loop cycle (2 weeks)Gate log entry with sign-off (Part 11)
QuarterlySafety drill, red-team refresh, review of new regulatory guidance
YearlyExternal security audit; review of the obligation map with counsel
Before any larger training runRe-run ai_act_check.py; plan for systemic-risk duties if near the threshold

14. Clauses that carry the promises

ClauseWhat it saysBacked by
Data useRaw customer code is never used for training; abstracted skills only with consentPart 8 pipeline and manifest
RemovalSkills derived from a customer's tasks are removed on request from future trainingManifest and skill-library ids
ResidencyProcessing in named regionsSandbox and provider configuration
IncidentsNotification within stated hoursPart 13 incident process
Sub-processorsGPU and cloud providers listed; changes notifiedPart 4 contracts
Model changesNotice before model updates; rollback availablePart 11 gate, Part 15 rollout
  • Never promise what the system cannot show.
    • Each clause has a row in the evidence library; legal and engineering review it together.

15. Beyond the EU

  • Rules differ by country and change often.
    • Many jurisdictions regulate how AI is used (deployers) more than how models are built, and sector rules (finance, health) add their own duties.
    • Gopala keeps one obligation map per market his customers operate in, reviewed yearly with local counsel.
  • The series stays global for now.
    • Localised guidance (for example for India) is planned as a separate section later in the site.

16. Who owns compliance as the company grows

  • Today: Gopala, with counsel and agents drafting.
  • At about 15 people: a part-time compliance and security lead.
    • Owns the evidence library, questionnaires and audits; the founder still signs releases.
  • At larger scale: separate safety, security and legal functions.
    • The release gate gains independent reviewers who did not build the model.

17. Seven approval mistakes

  • Treating compliance as paperwork after launch.
  • Assuming a small model has no obligations.
  • Writing the training-data summary from memory instead of a manifest.
  • Answering each customer questionnaire from scratch.
  • Promising "we never train on your data" without checking the pipeline.
  • Releasing to everyone at once.
  • Taking legal conclusions from a blog post (including this one).

18. Delegation box
